question:
Patient note:
A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department late this afternoon after noticing three episodes of jet-black, foul-smelling stools over the preceding 18 hours, the last of which stained the water a dark ink color and was accompanied by mild crampy discomfort in the epigastrium. He explained that he first observed an unusual charcoal hue when he wiped early this morning but dismissed it as dietary until the smell and stickiness became unmistakable after lunch; alarmed, he drove himself to the hospital. While in the waiting area he did not vomit and reported no bright red material per rectum, hematemesis, or coffee-ground emesis. He specifically denied dizziness, blurred vision on rising, presyncope, actual loss of consciousness, chest pain, palpitations, or dyspnea. Over-the-counter analgesics have been his only medications: he estimates taking 600 mg of ibuprofen every six hours for four consecutive days to ease a right ankle sprain sustained during recreational basketball. He has no prior history of peptic ulcer disease, gastrointestinal bleeding, hematologic disorders, pancreatitis, or chronic viral infections, and he has never undergone endoscopy. He consumes two to three beers on weekends, quit smoking cigarettes more than a decade ago, and has never used intravenous or intranasal drugs. There is no family history of bleeding diathesis, cirrhosis, or inflammatory bowel disease. Review of systems was otherwise negative for fevers, chills, weight loss, night sweats, easy bruising, pruritus, scleral discoloration, abdominal distention, or swelling of the lower limbs. On arrival he appeared anxious but was seated upright conversing normally. Initial vital signs, confirmed on repeat a few minutes later, showed a blood pressure of 135 / 78 mm Hg, a regular but rapid pulse of 108 beats per minute, respirations 18 per minute, temperature 37.0 °C, and oxygen saturation 99 % breathing ambient air. Conjunctival sacs were well perfused, mucous membranes were moist, and skin turgor was preserved; there was no icterus, spider angiomata, palmar erythema, digital clubbing, or gynecomastia. Jugular venous pulsation was not elevated, carotid upstrokes were brisk, and peripheral pulses were palpable symmetrically. Cardiac auscultation revealed normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; breath sounds were vesicular and clear. The abdomen was soft and nondistended with mild tenderness localized to the epigastrium but no guarding, rebound, or palpable mass; percussion suggested normal liver span and no shifting dullness. Bowel sounds were slightly hyperactive. There was no costovertebral angle tenderness and no peripheral edema. Digital rectal examination yielded a smear of thick, tarry stool that instantly turned the guaiac test strip dark blue. Laboratory samples drawn before any intravenous fluids or medications demonstrated hemoglobin 16.1 g/dL, hematocrit 47 %, mean corpuscular volume 88 fL, platelet count 268 × 10³ /µL, white blood cell count 7.9 × 10³ /µL, blood urea nitrogen 38 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, glucose 102 mg/dL, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, AST 28 U/L, ALT 31 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 96 U/L, albumin 4.2 g/dL, and an INR of 1.01. Upright chest radiograph showed no free subdiaphragmatic air and a normal cardiac silhouette; abdominal plain film revealed nonspecific gas pattern without obstruction. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram displayed sinus tachycardia at 108 bpm with no ischemic changes. The patient was attached to continuous cardiac and pulse oximetry monitoring, two large-bore peripheral IV catheters were sited but no crystalloid had been infused, and he remained conversational, oriented, and hemodynamically stable while awaiting further assessment by the gastroenterology team for probable upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Apply the Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score using pretreatment values:
- Blood urea: BUN 38 mg/dL × 0.357 ≈ 13.6 mmol/L urea, in the 10 to <25 mmol/L band → 4.
- Hemoglobin: 16.1 g/dL in a man, at or above 13 g/dL → 0.
- Systolic pressure: 135 mmHg, at or above 110 mmHg → 0.
- Pulse ≥100/min: 108/min → 1.
- Melena: black, tarry stool confirmed on rectal examination → 1.
- Syncope (2 points if present): denied → 0.
- Hepatic disease (2 if present): not evident → 0.
- Cardiac failure (2 if present): not evident → 0.
Total = 4 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 6.
Final answer: 6
